established.note: Standard material with a literature behind it. The references given are for orientation; check them before citing.

itd.title: Interaural time difference (ITD)
itd.grounding: Rayleigh (1907) for the duplex account. Woodworth's ray-tracing approximation is standard. Kuhn (1977, JASA) on its frequency dependence. Wightman and Kistler (1992, JASA) on low-frequency ITD dominating localization judgements.
itd.short: The difference in arrival time between the two ears. The dominant direction cue below about 1.5 kHz.
itd.body:
Sound from the right reaches the right ear first. The maximum for a human head is roughly 0.6 to 0.7 ms, at 90° [[azimuth]].

The auditory system extracts it by comparing the **fine timing** of the waveform at low frequencies, and the timing of the **envelope** at high frequencies. Fine-structure comparison fails above roughly 1.5 kHz because neurons stop phase-locking to individual cycles, and because half a wavelength becomes shorter than the head, making the comparison ambiguous. Above that, [[ild]] takes over: see [[duplex-theory]].

Human resolution is around 10 microseconds, finer than one sample at 44.1 kHz, which is why a renderer needs [[fractional-delay]].

ild.title: Interaural level difference (ILD)
ild.grounding: Rayleigh (1907). Standard treatment in Blauert, Spatial Hearing (MIT Press).
ild.short: The difference in loudness between the ears, caused by the head shadowing the far ear. Dominant above about 1.5 kHz.
ild.body:
Strongly frequency dependent, because shadowing depends on the ratio of wavelength to head size. Low frequencies [[diffraction|diffract]] around the head almost unimpeded; high frequencies are blocked.

Measured off this instrument's model at 90° [[azimuth]]: about +1.3 dB at 200–500 Hz, +7.8 dB at 1–2 kHz, and +15.2 dB at 4–8 kHz.

That frequency dependence has a direct consequence for [[decorrelation]]: there is little ILD in the bass, so a decorrelated low end has almost no cue to carry a position and tends to sound vague rather than wide. See [[bass-coherence]].

duplex-theory.title: Duplex theory
duplex-theory.grounding: Rayleigh (1907), 'On our perception of sound direction', Philosophical Magazine. Re-examined by Macpherson and Middlebrooks (2002, JASA), who show the two cues are weighted flexibly rather than switched between.
duplex-theory.short: Low frequencies are localized by timing, high frequencies by level.
duplex-theory.body:
[[itd]] dominates below roughly 1.5 kHz, where fine structure can be compared between the ears and the head is small relative to the wavelength. [[ild]] dominates above, where [[head-shadow|shadowing]] is substantial and phase comparison has become ambiguous.

The modern picture is less tidy: envelope ITDs remain usable at high frequencies, and the cues are weighted according to their reliability rather than switched between. The duplex split remains the right first approximation and explains why both cues must be modelled.

binaural.title: Binaural
binaural.short: Involving both ears, and specifically the differences between them.
binaural.body:
Human direction hearing rests mostly on comparing the two ear signals. Binaural audio means audio produced so those signals resemble what a real scene would have delivered, which is why it works properly only on headphones: loudspeakers deliver each channel to both ears and destroy the comparison.

The two main comparisons are [[itd]] and [[ild]]. See [[duplex-theory]].

azimuth.title: Azimuth
azimuth.short: Horizontal angle around the listener. Here 0° is straight ahead and positive is to the right.
azimuth.body:
One of two angles needed to specify a direction; the other is [[elevation]]. 90° is directly right, 180° directly behind, 270° to the left.

The sign convention varies between publications and datasets, so check it before comparing numbers with another system.

elevation.title: Elevation
elevation.grounding: Standard; see Middlebrooks and Green (1991, Annual Review of Psychology) for a review of the cues involved.
elevation.short: Vertical angle, above or below the horizontal plane.
elevation.body:
Carried almost entirely by [[spectral-cues]] from the [[pinna]], not by [[itd]] or [[ild]], since a sound directly above produces no interaural difference at all.

This instrument works purely on the horizontal plane. The [[spherical-head-model]] has no pinna, so it cannot synthesize elevation.

median-plane.title: Median plane
median-plane.short: The vertical plane splitting the head into left and right halves.
median-plane.body: Directions on it, straight ahead, straight up, straight behind, produce zero [[itd]] and zero [[ild]] on a symmetric head. Localization within it therefore depends entirely on [[spectral-cues]], which is why it is much less precise than left-right judgement and why [[front-back-confusion]] lives there.

interaural-axis.title: Interaural axis
interaural-axis.body: [[itd]] and [[ild]] are maximal for sources on this axis and zero for sources on the [[median-plane]]. What the two-eared comparison really encodes is angle from this axis, which is the geometric root of the [[cone-of-confusion]].

head-shadow.title: Head shadow
head-shadow.short: The head blocking sound from reaching the far ear, more strongly at high frequencies.
head-shadow.body:
The physical cause of [[ild]]. Because it depends on wavelength relative to head size, it acts as a frequency-dependent attenuation rather than a flat one, so a plausible model needs a **filter** and not a gain.

This instrument uses the [[brown-duda-shadow]] one-pole/one-zero approximation.

diffraction.title: Diffraction
diffraction.short: Waves bending around obstacles when the wavelength is comparable to or larger than the obstacle.
diffraction.body:
A 100 Hz tone has a wavelength of about 3.4 m, far larger than a head, so it bends around almost unimpeded. An 8 kHz tone has a wavelength of about 4 cm and is blocked, casting an acoustic shadow.

This is why [[ild]] grows with frequency, and why the bass has the fewest spatial cues available.

pinna.title: Pinna
pinna.grounding: Batteau (1967) on the pinna's role in localization; Middlebrooks and Green (1991) for review.
pinna.short: The external ear. Its folds filter incoming sound direction-dependently.
pinna.body:
The folds create direction-dependent notches and peaks, mostly above 5 kHz. These [[spectral-cues]] resolve [[elevation]] and [[front-back-confusion]], neither of which [[itd]] or [[ild]] can settle.

Pinnae are highly individual, which is the main reason a generic [[hrtf]] performs worse than your own. A sphere has no pinna, which is why the [[analytic-hrtf]] here has no elevation and complete front-back confusion.

spectral-cues.title: Spectral cues
spectral-cues.short: Direction-dependent peaks and notches imposed by the pinna, head and torso.
spectral-cues.body:
Monaural in principle: one ear alone carries them. They are the only cues available for [[elevation]] and for distinguishing front from back, since those directions can share identical [[itd]] and [[ild]].

They are also fragile: they live at high frequencies, need broadband content to be visible, and are individual enough that another person's [[hrtf]] supplies the wrong ones.

cone-of-confusion.title: Cone of confusion
cone-of-confusion.grounding: Standard geometric consequence of the two-cue system; see Blauert, Spatial Hearing.
cone-of-confusion.short: The set of directions sharing the same ITD and ILD. A cone around the interaural axis.
cone-of-confusion.body:
Because [[itd]] and [[ild]] encode angle from the [[interaural-axis]], every direction on a cone around that axis produces the same pair of values. Front and back at mirror-image angles are the simplest case.

Real listeners resolve it with [[spectral-cues]] and, decisively, with [[head-movement-cue|head movement]]. This instrument has neither.

head-movement-cue.title: Head movement as a cue
head-movement-cue.grounding: Wallach (1940), 'The role of head movements and vestibular and visual cues in sound localization', Journal of Experimental Psychology.
head-movement-cue.short: Small head turns resolve front-back ambiguity, because the cues change in opposite directions.
head-movement-cue.body:
Turn your head slightly left: a source in front moves right in ear-relative terms, a source behind moves left. That difference disambiguates the [[cone-of-confusion]] immediately, and listeners do it constantly without noticing.

Static headphone playback removes it entirely, which is much of why [[front-back-confusion]] and in-head localization are worse over headphones than in life. Head tracking is the fix and is not implemented here.

localization.title: Localization
localization.body:
Distinguish it from [[lateralization]], which places a sound on a line inside the head, and from [[externalization]], which is whether it is outside the head at all. The three are routinely conflated and come apart in practice.

For this instrument the operative question is not how accurate localization is but whether it occurs. See [[the-question]].

lateralization.title: Lateralization
lateralization.short: Hearing a sound at a position along the line between your ears, inside your head.
lateralization.body:
What headphones give by default: a position on a left-right axis through the skull rather than out in the world.

The distinction matters because [[itd]] and [[ild]] alone mostly buy lateralization. Getting a sound outside the head needs plausible [[spectral-cues]], usually some reverberation, and ideally head movement.

externalization.title: Externalization
externalization.short: Whether a sound is heard outside the head rather than inside it.
externalization.body:
Largely independent of direction accuracy: a sound can be clearly to the left and still inside the skull. Helped by individualized [[hrtf|HRTFs]], realistic [[spectral-cues]], room reflections, head tracking, and [[headphone-compensation]].

Worth tracking separately in listening notes: a field that is diffuse and enveloping but stubbornly inside the head is a different result from one that is outside and enveloping.

auditory-memory.title: Memory for spatial quality
auditory-memory.grounding: General finding in psychoacoustics that fine timbral and spatial detail decays quickly; the practical consequence is standard in audio comparison methodology, for example ITU-R BS.1116 recommending rapid switching.
auditory-memory.short: Short. This is why rapid switching between conditions is more sensitive than sequential listening.
auditory-memory.body:
Fine detail of timbre and spatial quality decays quickly, so comparing two renders played one after another with a gap between them is much less sensitive than switching between them mid-note.

That is the reason every [[variant]] is rendered over the same span and sample aligned. It is also why [[level-matching]] is non-negotiable: a level difference is easy to remember across a gap and will dominate the judgement.

hrtf.title: Head-related transfer function (HRTF)
hrtf.grounding: Wightman and Kistler (1989, JASA) on measurement and validation of free-field-to-eardrum transfer functions. Blauert, Spatial Hearing, for the general treatment.
hrtf.short: The filter describing how a direction's sound is transformed on its way to each eardrum.
hrtf.body:
One filter per ear per direction, bundling [[itd]], [[ild]], and the [[spectral-cues]] from [[pinna]], head and torso. Convolve a mono signal with a direction's pair and it appears to come from that direction over headphones.

In the time domain the same information is the [[hrir]]. HRTFs are either **measured** on a real or dummy head and stored as [[sofa]] files, or **synthesized** from a physical model, which is what the [[analytic-hrtf]] does.

hrir.title: Head-related impulse response (HRIR)
hrir.short: The time-domain form of an HRTF: a short pair of impulse responses, one per ear.
hrir.body:
The [[hrtf]] and the HRIR are the same information related by a Fourier transform. Rendering works in the time domain, [[convolution|convolving]] the source signal with the pair for its current [[azimuth]].

In this instrument each is 128 taps by default, synthesized on a one-degree grid; both are adjustable.

spherical-head-model.title: Spherical head model
spherical-head-model.grounding: The rigid-sphere scattering solution is classical (Rayleigh). Duda and Martens (1998, JASA) give the modern treatment for HRTF purposes.
spherical-head-model.short: Treating the head as a rigid sphere with two ears on it.
spherical-head-model.body:
The simplest object producing both an [[itd]] and a frequency-dependent [[ild]], and one whose scattering has a known solution. That makes it the natural base for a synthetic [[hrtf]].

Its limits are the limits of the abstraction: a sphere is front-back symmetric and has no [[pinna]], so it cannot produce [[spectral-cues]], [[elevation]], or front-back discrimination.

woodworth-model.title: Woodworth ITD formula
woodworth-model.grounding: Woodworth and Schlosberg, Experimental Psychology. The ray-tracing form is standard and widely reproduced; Kuhn (1977, JASA) documents where it departs from measurement at low frequencies.
woodworth-model.short: A ray-tracing approximation for interaural time difference on a sphere.
woodworth-model.body:
ITD = (a/c)·(θ + sin θ), where a is [[head-radius|head radius]], c the [[speed-of-sound]], and θ the angle from the [[median-plane]]. The two terms are the extra straight-line distance and the extra distance around the curve of the head.

With a = 8.75 cm it gives 0.656 ms at 90° [[azimuth]], which matches measurement well. It is a low-frequency approximation, since true ITD is somewhat frequency dependent.

**It is front-back symmetric by construction**, which is the origin of this instrument's [[front-back-confusion]].

brown-duda-shadow.title: Brown and Duda head-shadow filter
brown-duda-shadow.grounding: Brown and Duda (1998), 'A structural model for binaural sound synthesis', IEEE Transactions on Speech and Audio Processing 6(5).
brown-duda-shadow.short: A one-pole/one-zero filter approximating the head's frequency-dependent shadowing.
brown-duda-shadow.body:
A first-order shelving filter: unity gain at DC, a corner near c/a (roughly 600 Hz for a human head), and a high-frequency gain that varies with the angle between the source and that ear's outward normal.

That gain runs from about 2.0 at the near ear (+6 dB) to 0.1 at the far ear (−20 dB). The angle-dependent, frequency-dependent gain **is** the [[ild]] cue.

Cheap, stable and perceptually convincing, which is why a structural model like this remains useful even though exact sphere solutions exist.

analytic-hrtf.title: The synthesized HRTF used here
analytic-hrtf.short: An HRTF built from a physical model rather than measured. What this instrument uses by default.
analytic-hrtf.body:
Three pieces: the [[woodworth-model]] for [[itd]], the [[brown-duda-shadow]] filter for [[ild]], and a [[fractional-delay]] to realise the timing precisely. No dataset needed, works at any [[azimuth]], and gives correct ITD with plausible ILD.

What it does **not** give: [[pinna]] cues, and therefore no [[elevation]] and complete [[front-back-confusion]]. It is also not [[individualization|individualized]].

Adequate to hear rotation and diffuseness. Not adequate to settle rotation direction.

head-radius.title: Head radius
head-radius.short: The single anthropometric parameter of the head model. Default 8.75 cm.
head-radius.body:
Feeds directly into the [[woodworth-model]], where it scales the whole [[itd]] curve, and into the [[brown-duda-shadow]] filter, where it sets the corner frequency at c/a.

A larger head gives larger interaural delays and shifts the shadowing corner down. Population values run roughly 8 to 9.5 cm. Adjusting it is the closest this model comes to [[individualization]], though it captures only the crudest part of what makes a real head individual.

speed-of-sound.title: Speed of sound
speed-of-sound.short: 343 m/s by default, for dry air at about 20°C.
speed-of-sound.body:
Appears in the [[woodworth-model]] as the conversion from distance to time, and in the [[brown-duda-shadow]] corner frequency c/a.

It varies with temperature by roughly 0.6 m/s per degree Celsius. Exposed mainly for completeness: within any plausible range the effect on the rendered cues is small compared to the effect of [[head-radius]].

sofa.title: SOFA files and measured HRTFs
sofa.grounding: SOFA is standardised as AES69. Public datasets: SADIE II (University of York), SONICOM, and CIPIC (Algazi et al., 2001).
sofa.short: The standard container for measured HRTF datasets.
sofa.body:
Spatially Oriented Format for Acoustics. Holds [[hrir|HRIRs]] for many measured directions together with the geometry describing where each was taken.

Moving to measured data would change this project more than any other single upgrade, because it brings [[pinna]] [[spectral-cues]] and therefore real front-back discrimination, which is what currently makes rotation direction unanswerable.

The code has a drop-in class with an identical interface. The substantial work is [[hrtf-interpolation]].

hrtf-interpolation.title: HRIR interpolation
hrtf-interpolation.grounding: The ITD-alignment approach is standard practice; see for example Hartung, Braasch and Sterbing (1999) on interpolation methods for HRTF datasets.
hrtf-interpolation.short: Getting an HRIR for a direction between two measured ones. Harder than it appears.
hrtf-interpolation.body:
Measured sets are on a grid, but sources move continuously. Naive crossfading between neighbouring [[hrir|HRIRs]] causes [[comb-filtering]], because the two have different arrival times and averaging them sums two copies at slightly different delays.

The standard fix: separate the [[itd]] first, interpolate the magnitude response only, then reapply the delay. The [[sofa]] class here uses nearest-neighbour lookup instead, which is safe but quantises source positions to the measurement grid.

individualization.title: Individualized HRTFs
individualization.grounding: Wenzel, Arruda, Kistler and Wightman (1993, JASA) on localization using non-individualized HRTFs.
individualization.short: Using your own head and ears rather than someone else's.
individualization.body:
[[pinna]] shapes vary enormously, so a generic [[hrtf]] supplies [[spectral-cues]] that do not match the ones a listener learned. The usual consequences are worse [[elevation]], more [[front-back-confusion]], and poorer [[externalization]].

For this project it matters less than it might, since the target percept concerns the field as a whole rather than precise positions. It becomes important as soon as listeners must agree about direction.

distance-hearing.title: Distance hearing
distance-hearing.grounding: Zahorik, Brungart and Bronkhorst (2005, Acta Acustica) review auditory distance perception. Brungart and Rabinowitz (1999, JASA) on nearby sources and the near-field ILD. Duda and Martens (1998, JASA) for the rigid-sphere near field.
distance-hearing.short: Perceived distance rests on level, reverberation, spectrum, and near-field binaural changes.
distance-hearing.body:
Level alone is ambiguous, since a quiet nearby source and a loud distant one can produce the same intensity at the ear. In rooms the strongest cue is the direct-to-reverberant ratio, which requires reverberation. Long paths attenuate high frequencies. Within roughly a metre the [[ild]] grows well beyond its far-field value, including at low frequencies where [[head-shadow]] contributes little, because the source-to-ear path lengths differ proportionally more.

A renderer without reverberation therefore conveys distance weakly, through level and near-field ILD alone. See [[source-distance]] for what this instrument implements.

head-tracking.title: Head tracking
head-tracking.grounding: The benefit follows from Wallach (1940) on head movements; dynamic-cue benefits in virtual auditory display are documented by Wightman and Kistler (1999, JASA) among others.
head-tracking.short: Updating the rendered scene as the listener's head turns.
head-tracking.body:
Restores the [[head-movement-cue]], the most reliable resolver of [[front-back-confusion]] and a large contributor to [[externalization]].

Not implemented here. For this project it would be valuable and also awkward: it makes rotation direction answerable, but it hands the listener an active strategy for probing the field, which may alter the very percept under study.

headphone-compensation.title: Headphone compensation
headphone-compensation.short: Filtering out the headphone's own frequency response so it does not add to the HRTF.
headphone-compensation.body:
Headphones impose their own colouration on top of the rendered [[hrtf]], corrupting the [[spectral-cues]] that carry [[elevation]] and front-back information.

A related and more immediately damaging problem: **operating-system spatializers**. Windows Sonic and Dolby Atmos for Headphones apply a second head model on top of this one. Switch them off, or every measurement describes the wrong system.

auditory-motion.title: Auditory motion perception
auditory-motion.grounding: Grantham (1986, JASA) on detection and discrimination of simulated motion. Carlile and Leung (2016, Trends in Hearing), 'The perception of auditory motion', is a recent review covering the snapshot debate.
auditory-motion.short: How the auditory system detects that a sound is moving. Whether a dedicated mechanism exists is disputed.
auditory-motion.body:
The dominant account is a **snapshot** one: position is estimated at successive instants and motion inferred from the change. On that account there is no dedicated motion detector, and motion perception is parasitic on [[localization]].

The evidence is mixed. Motion-specific effects such as an auditory [[motion-aftereffect]] have been reported, which is hard to explain with snapshots alone, but the field has not settled.

This unsettledness is what makes the project's [[the-question|central question]] worth asking.

snapshot-hypothesis.title: Snapshot hypothesis
snapshot-hypothesis.grounding: Associated with Grantham; discussed as the default account in Carlile and Leung (2016).
snapshot-hypothesis.short: That motion is inferred by comparing successive static position estimates.
snapshot-hypothesis.body:
It predicts that motion sensitivity should be limited by position sensitivity, and that anything unlocalizable should be unable to appear to move.

That prediction is what makes an unlocalizable rotating field a useful test case rather than merely an unusual effect.

mama.title: Minimum audible movement angle
mama.grounding: Perrott and Musicant (1977, JASA), 'Minimum auditory movement angle'. Later work establishes its dependence on velocity.
mama.short: The smallest arc a source must traverse before the movement is detected.
mama.body:
Larger than the minimum audible *angle* between two static sources, and it grows with velocity: faster motion needs more arc before it registers.

Practical consequence for choosing a rotation rate: too slow and nothing is detectable within a listening window; too fast and the percept smears into fluttering texture rather than motion.

binaural-sluggishness.title: Binaural sluggishness
binaural-sluggishness.grounding: Grantham and Wightman (1978, JASA) on detectability of varying interaural differences. Also Blauert (1972) on the lag of lateralization. Estimates of the effective integration window vary considerably by paradigm.
binaural-sluggishness.short: The binaural system integrates over a long window and cannot follow fast changes in interaural cues.
binaural-sluggishness.body:
Estimates of the effective integration time run to the order of a hundred milliseconds or more, far slower than monaural temporal resolution. Fast fluctuations in [[itd]] or interaural coherence are smoothed rather than tracked.

This sets a ceiling on how fast a field can rotate and still be heard as rotating rather than as texture.

motion-aftereffect.title: Auditory motion aftereffect
motion-aftereffect.grounding: Grantham (1989, Perception and Psychophysics) reports aftereffects with horizontally moving free-field sources. The effect is weaker and less consistently replicated than its visual counterpart, and its interpretation is contested.
motion-aftereffect.short: After prolonged exposure to motion in one direction, a stationary sound can seem to drift the other way.
motion-aftereffect.body:
The auditory analogue of the visual waterfall illusion.

It matters here because an aftereffect implies direction-selective adaptation, which implies something more like a motion detector than a chain of [[snapshot-hypothesis|snapshots]]. An aftereffect produced by an unlocalizable rotating field would be a much stronger result than a description task, because it does not depend on a listener's report of a subtle quality.

random-dot-kinematogram.title: Random-dot kinematogram
random-dot-kinematogram.grounding: Braddick (1974, Vision Research) introduced the paradigm. Newsome and Paré (1988, Journal of Neuroscience) established the link to area MT via lesions; Britten, Shadlen, Newsome and Movshon (1992, Journal of Neuroscience) compared neuronal and psychophysical sensitivity. Motion coherence threshold is a standard measure.
random-dot-kinematogram.short: A visual stimulus in which the direction of an ensemble is reported while any single element carries almost none of it.
random-dot-kinematogram.body:
A field of dots, some proportion moving in a common direction and the rest moving at random. Observers report the global direction reliably well below the proportion at which any single dot can be followed, so the motion is extracted by pooling across elements; see [[global-motion]].

Two properties of the stimulus are worth stating exactly, since they bound what it can be used to argue. The dots move, and their coherence lies in a shared direction of travel. Every dot also stays visible and localizable throughout: what the experimenter varies is how many dots share a direction, never whether a dot has a position.

That second property is where the auditory parallel stops. The manipulation transfers directly as the [[motion-coherence|motion coherence share]], which is the one place the analogy is close. [[decorrelation|Decorrelation]] removes a source's position altogether and has no counterpart in this stimulus; see [[the-analogy]].

global-motion.title: Global motion
global-motion.grounding: Well established in vision, with identified neural substrate in area MT/V5. See Newsome and Paré (1988) and Born and Bradley (2005, Annual Review of Neuroscience) for review.
global-motion.short: Motion as a property of an ensemble, pooled across elements rather than tracked in any one.
global-motion.body:
In vision this is a distinct level of processing with an identified substrate, probed by the [[random-dot-kinematogram]]: the direction of an ensemble is available even where the trajectory of any one element is uninformative.

What it establishes is that motion perception can proceed by pooling rather than by tracking an individual. It leaves open whether motion can be perceived when the elements have no recoverable position at all, since the dots in the paradigm always have one.

Whether an auditory equivalent exists is unestablished, and there is a structural asymmetry to reckon with. Vision resolves many independent spatial channels while hearing reconstructs space from a two-channel comparison, so any auditory pooling would operate on [[interaural-statistics|interaural statistics]] rather than on a spatial map.

front-back-confusion.title: Front-back confusion
front-back-confusion.grounding: Standard consequence of the cone of confusion; rates in headphone listening with non-individualized HRTFs are documented in Wenzel et al. (1993, JASA).
front-back-confusion.short: Mistaking a sound in front for one behind. Complete in this instrument, by construction.
front-back-confusion.body:
The [[woodworth-model]] is front-back symmetric: [[azimuth]] 0° and 180° produce identical [[hrir|HRIRs]], as do 45°/135° and 225°/315°. A sphere has no [[pinna]], so there are no [[spectral-cues]] to break the tie.

**The consequence for this project is specific.** A full 360° rotation produces an interaural pattern that completes **twice**, so it is indistinguishable from a left-right oscillation at double the rate, and rotation direction cannot be recovered. See [[interaural-pattern-rate]].

So 'is it turning, and which way' is confounded here, while 'can you point at anything' is not. Design listening tests around the second.

interaural-pattern-rate.title: Interaural pattern rate
interaural-pattern-rate.short: The rate at which the interaural cue pattern repeats: twice the lap rate under this head model.
interaural-pattern-rate.body:
A ring turning at R degrees per second completes R/360 laps per second. Because of [[front-back-confusion]] the interaural pattern repeats twice per lap, so the pattern rate is R/180 Hz.

This is the frequency the [[rotation-signature]] measure examines. With [[sofa|measured HRTFs]] the factor of two disappears.

rotation-rate.title: Rotation rate
rotation-rate.short: How fast a lattice turns about the head, in degrees per second.
rotation-rate.body:
Bounded below by [[mama]] and above by [[binaural-sluggishness]].

In practice: slow drift around 30°/s, clear rotation between roughly 60 and 120°/s, and past a few hundred it stops reading as motion. These are working figures from listening here rather than published thresholds.

Rotation is the one motion measured in degrees, and the only one with a fixed cyclic rate for a measure to look for; see [[interaural-pattern-rate]]. [[radial-flow]] and [[translation]] are set in metres per second, and their usable range depends on the size of the lattice as well as on the speed.

coherence.title: Coherence
coherence.short: How similar two signals are, as a number between 0 and 1.
coherence.body:
Two identical signals are perfectly coherent; two independent noise signals are incoherent. In between is a continuum, which this instrument treats as a continuous control.

Be careful with the word: **inter-source** coherence (between two source signals) and **interaural** coherence (between the two ears) are different quantities, and both are reported. See [[coherence-matrix]] and [[iacc]].

correlation-coefficient.title: Correlation coefficient
correlation-coefficient.short: A normalized measure of linear similarity, from −1 through 0 to +1.
correlation-coefficient.body:
Subtract the means, multiply sample by sample, sum, and normalize by both signals' energies. +1 means identical up to a positive scale, −1 inverted, 0 unrelated.

Normalization is what makes it a similarity measure rather than a level measure. Both [[iacc]] and the [[coherence-matrix]] are correlation coefficients, differing in what they compare and whether a time lag is allowed.

decorrelation.title: Decorrelation
decorrelation.grounding: Kendall (1995), 'The decorrelation of audio signals and its impact on spatial imagery', Computer Music Journal 19(4), is the standard reference for the technique and its perceptual effects.
decorrelation.short: Making copies of a signal that sound the same but no longer align with each other.
decorrelation.body:
Filter each copy so they become mutually incoherent while each stays approximately [[allpass-filter|allpass]], meaning essentially unchanged in [[magnitude-spectrum]] and therefore in timbre.

It is the standard tool for producing width and [[envelopment]] from a mono source, and here it is also what makes individual sources unlocatable.

What matters is the resulting [[coherence-matrix|coherence structure]]; the filter design is how you realise it.

decorrelation-amount.title: Decorrelation amount
decorrelation-amount.short: The master coherence control. 0 is identical copies, 1 is maximally decorrelated.
decorrelation-amount.body:
A blend between the original signal and its decorrelated version, applied per source so that the sources become independent of one another as well as of the input.

It is set on the variant and may be overridden on any [[component]], which is what lets a near group stay coherent inside a diffuse far one, or the reverse.

Level is held constant across the whole sweep. This is not automatic: a plain blend dips several decibels in the middle because the two components partially cancel, which would make the control change loudness as well as coherence. See [[level-matching]].

coherence-matrix.title: Coherence matrix
coherence-matrix.short: Measured pairwise correlation between every pair of sources: what was achieved, as opposed to what was requested.
coherence-matrix.body:
An N×N table with 1.0 on the diagonal. Off-diagonal entries near 0 mean the sources are mutually independent; near 1 means they are still effectively copies.

It reports what was achieved rather than what was asked for, a distinction that matters because the [[decorrelation-amount]] is a request while the filters themselves are random draws; see [[noise-floor]].

The matrix varies over time whenever the amount does, whether through [[coherence-lfo|modulation]] or through components carrying different amounts, so a single snapshot is not a summary. It is sampled at several instants and the range reported.

velvet-noise.title: Velvet noise
velvet-noise.grounding: Karjalainen and Järveläinen (2007) on reverberation modelling using velvet noise. Välimäki, Parker, Savioja, Smith and Abel (2012, IEEE TASLP), 'Fifty years of artificial reverberation', for context; Välimäki et al. (2017) on filtered velvet noise.
velvet-noise.short: A sparse sequence of +1 and −1 impulses at jittered positions. Spectrally flat and nearly colourless.
velvet-noise.body:
Sparse, so convolution with it is cheap; random in sign and jittered in position, so it is spectrally flat without the ringing that regular delay patterns produce. Being sparse, it leaves transients relatively intact.

As [[impulse-density]] rises, every sample eventually carries an impulse and the sequence becomes a random sign sequence, which is essentially the [[allpass-filter]] case.

allpass-filter.title: Allpass filter and random-phase noise
allpass-filter.grounding: Allpass structures for decorrelation and reverberation go back to Schroeder (1962, JAES). Random-phase construction is standard practice.
allpass-filter.short: A filter that passes every frequency at equal level while changing their relative timing.
allpass-filter.body:
Allpass means the [[magnitude-spectrum]] is unchanged and only the [[phase-spectrum]] is altered, which is exactly what [[decorrelation]] wants: destroy the alignment between copies without changing what each sounds like.

The implementation here builds a spectrum of unit magnitude and random phase and transforms it back. Because energy is spread across the whole response rather than concentrated in a few impulses, it smears transients more than [[velvet-noise]] does.

phase-depth.title: Phase randomization depth
phase-depth.short: How far the allpass filter scrambles phase, from none to fully random.
phase-depth.body: At 0 the filter is an identity and there is no decorrelation. At 1 phases are uniform over the full range. Intermediate values give partial scrambling, so coherence falls smoothly as it rises.

ir-length.title: IR length
ir-length.short: Length of the decorrelating impulse response, so how far the signal is smeared in time.
ir-length.body:
Longer means more thoroughly decorrelated and more temporal smearing, which transients suffer from.

Measured here, inter-source coherence runs from about 0.19 at 5 ms to 0.04 at 120 ms: a large effect relative to the measurement [[noise-floor]], and the filter-shape control most worth sweeping. Compare [[impulse-density]], which saturates.

impulse-density.title: Impulse density
impulse-density.short: How many impulses per second fill the velvet IR.
impulse-density.body:
A large effect while sparse and inert once dense: see [[density-saturation]] for the measured curve.

In the sparse region the [[ir-envelope]] dominates the outcome, which is worth knowing before attributing an effect to density.

ir-envelope.title: IR envelope
ir-envelope.short: The amplitude shape over the decorrelating IR: flat, Hann-windowed, or exponentially decaying.
ir-envelope.body:
Separated out as its own control because it was previously a hidden variable: the velvet preset was flat and the allpass preset Hann-windowed, so comparing them on [[impulse-density]] was partly measuring the window. See [[envelope-confound]].

An exponential decay is what a real diffuse field's envelope looks like, so it is the most physically motivated of the three.

frequency-dependent-decorrelation.title: Frequency-dependent decorrelation
frequency-dependent-decorrelation.short: Decorrelating some frequency bands more than others.
frequency-dependent-decorrelation.body:
Set a [[crossover]] and a separate amount per band. The usual reason is [[bass-coherence]].

Bands are built as successive differences of lowpasses, so they telescope back to the input exactly. Uniform band amounts are therefore inert, and the control colours nothing until the bands actually differ.

bass-coherence.title: Keeping the bass coherent
bass-coherence.grounding: Standard practice in stereo and upmix processing; the rationale follows from the frequency dependence of ILD (see Blauert) and from mono-compatibility concerns in mastering.
bass-coherence.short: Decorrelate the highs, leave the lows alone.
bass-coherence.body:
The head does not [[head-shadow|shadow]] low frequencies, so there is little [[ild]] available and correspondingly little spatial information. Decorrelating the bass therefore does not make it wide, it makes it vague and weak, and it can cause level problems when channels partially cancel on summing.

The usual crossover sits in the low hundreds of hertz. Exposed here rather than fixed, because whether the practice holds for a **rotating** field is untested.

micro-delay.title: Micro-delay spread
micro-delay.short: Giving each source a slightly different delay. A crude decorrelator.
micro-delay.body:
Cheap and effective at breaking coherence, but it [[comb-filtering|comb filters]] when the sources sum, so it colours the sound in a way [[velvet-noise]] does not. Retained for comparison precisely because it colours differently.

Delay cannot be negative, so the spread runs from zero at the first source up to the set value at the last.

micro-pitch.title: Micro-pitch shift
micro-pitch.short: Detuning each source by a few cents. Another crude decorrelator.
micro-pitch.body:
Produces a chorus-like thickening, and decorrelates progressively: the further apart in pitch, the faster the copies drift out of phase.

Its crudeness is specific. Shifting pitch by resampling also changes duration, so over a long passage the sources drift out of **time** with each other, which becomes audible as smearing on rhythmic material.

coherence-lfo.title: Coherence modulation
coherence-lfo.short: Varying the decorrelation amount over time, so the field alternates between focused and diffuse.
coherence-lfo.body:
A low-frequency oscillator on the [[decorrelation-amount]], so a field moves between focused and diffuse across a passage rather than holding one coherence throughout.

Rate and depth are set separately, and a source spread offsets the oscillator's phase from one source to the next so that they do not all reach maximum coherence at the same instant. Level is held constant across the sweep, as it is for the fixed amount.

The usable rate has the same ceiling as motion does, since the binaural system integrates over a hundred milliseconds or more; see [[binaural-sluggishness]]. Faster modulation reads as texture rather than as the field changing focus.

impulse-response.title: Impulse response
impulse-response.short: What a system does to a single instantaneous click. It characterises the system completely.
impulse-response.body:
For any linear time-invariant system, the impulse response is a full description: the output for any input follows from it by [[convolution]].

That is why so much here is expressed as impulse responses: the [[hrir]] is the impulse response of the path from a direction to your eardrum, and the decorrelating filters are impulse responses designed to be allpass but mutually dissimilar.

convolution.title: Convolution
convolution.short: The operation that applies an impulse response to a signal.
convolution.body:
Slide the [[impulse-response]] along the signal, multiply, and sum. Every output sample is a weighted combination of recent input samples, with the impulse response supplying the weights.

Direct convolution costs proportionally to the product of the two lengths, so it is normally done by transforming both to the frequency domain, multiplying, and transforming back.

overlap-add.title: Overlap-add
overlap-add.short: Convolving a long signal in short overlapping blocks, then summing the results.
overlap-add.body:
Necessary here because the filter **changes over time** as sources move. Each block is convolved with the [[hrir]] for the [[azimuth]] at that block's centre.

Blocks are windowed and overlapped rather than butted together, because an abrupt filter change between adjacent blocks produces a click. The window must satisfy [[cola]] for the reconstruction to be transparent.

cola.title: Constant overlap-add (COLA)
cola.short: The condition that overlapping windows sum to a constant, so the reconstruction has no ripple.
cola.body:
If windows do not sum to a constant across the overlap, the output is amplitude-modulated at the block rate, audible as a buzz or tremolo.

A periodic [[hann-window]] at 50% overlap satisfies COLA exactly. Substituting the symmetric form, which differs by one sample, breaks it.

window-function.title: Window function
window-function.short: A taper applied to a block of samples so it fades in and out instead of starting abruptly.
window-function.body:
Cutting a block with hard edges introduces discontinuities, which spread energy across the whole spectrum. A window tapers the edges to zero.

In [[overlap-add]] the window also serves as the crossfade between successive filter settings, which is what keeps a moving source from clicking. Windows also appear as the [[ir-envelope]] on decorrelating filters, where the shape is a deliberate parameter.

hann-window.title: Hann window
hann-window.short: A raised-cosine taper. The standard choice, and it satisfies COLA at 50% overlap.
hann-window.body:
A single cosine lobe from 0 up to 1 and back to 0, smooth, with well-behaved spectral leakage.

The **periodic** form, which omits the duplicated endpoint, sums to exactly 1 at 50% overlap and therefore satisfies [[cola]]. The symmetric form does not, quite.

block-size.title: Block size
block-size.short: How many samples are processed at once, and therefore how often source positions update.
block-size.body:
Smaller blocks update the [[azimuth]] and the decorrelation amount more often, tracking motion more finely at higher cost. Larger blocks are cheaper and coarser.

The default of 256 samples with a 128-sample hop updates about 344 times per second at 44.1 kHz, far finer than [[binaural-sluggishness]] can follow, so it is not a perceptual limit in practice.

fractional-delay.title: Fractional delay
fractional-delay.grounding: Laakso, Välimäki, Karjalainen and Laine (1996, IEEE Signal Processing Magazine), 'Splitting the unit delay', is the standard survey.
fractional-delay.short: Delaying a signal by a non-integer number of samples.
fractional-delay.body:
Necessary because [[itd]] does not land on sample boundaries. At 44.1 kHz one sample is about 23 microseconds, while human interaural resolution is nearer 10, so rounding to the sample grid would be audibly coarse.

Realised here with a [[windowed-sinc]] interpolator.

windowed-sinc.title: Windowed sinc
windowed-sinc.short: The standard way to build an interpolating or band-limiting filter.
windowed-sinc.body:
The ideal interpolator is a sinc function, infinitely long and so unusable directly. Truncating abruptly causes ripple, so it is multiplied by a [[window-function]] that tapers it smoothly to zero.

One detail matters in this implementation: the window must be centred **on the delay**, not on the middle of the array. Centring it on the array truncates the sinc asymmetrically and destroys the high frequencies.

comb-filtering.title: Comb filtering
comb-filtering.short: The regular pattern of peaks and notches produced by summing a signal with a delayed copy of itself.
comb-filtering.body:
Some frequencies reinforce, others cancel, at regular intervals across the spectrum. The result is a hollow, metallic colouration.

It is the main colouration risk in this system: it appears when [[micro-delay|micro-delays]] are used as decorrelators, when [[hrtf-interpolation|HRIRs are interpolated naively]], and as the only audible effect of rotating a [[degenerate-ring]]. Avoiding it is much of why [[velvet-noise]] is preferred over delay-based decorrelation.

crossover.title: Crossover
crossover.short: A frequency at which a signal is split into bands for separate treatment.
crossover.body:
The usual difficulty is that the bands must sum back to the original without peaks or dips at the crossover point.

This instrument sidesteps it by constructing bands as successive differences of lowpasses, so they telescope back exactly regardless of the filter's phase behaviour. Used for [[frequency-dependent-decorrelation]] and in particular for [[bass-coherence]].

zero-phase-filter.title: Zero-phase filtering
zero-phase-filter.short: Filtering forwards and then backwards, so the result has no phase shift.
zero-phase-filter.body:
Every causal filter delays some frequencies more than others. Running the filter forwards then in reverse cancels that exactly, leaving magnitude shaping with no phase distortion.

Possible only offline, since it requires the whole signal in advance. Used for band splitting, where phase differences between bands would otherwise cause [[comb-filtering]] on recombination.

magnitude-spectrum.title: Magnitude spectrum
magnitude-spectrum.short: How much of each frequency a signal contains, ignoring timing.
magnitude-spectrum.body:
Broadly what determines timbre. Two signals with the same magnitude spectrum and different [[phase-spectrum|phases]] can sound very similar in character while being completely different waveforms.

That fact is the basis of [[decorrelation]]: an [[allpass-filter]] leaves magnitude untouched and scrambles only phase.

phase-spectrum.title: Phase spectrum
phase-spectrum.short: The relative timing of each frequency component.
phase-spectrum.body:
Hearing is relatively insensitive to the absolute phase of a steady sound, which is why scrambling it changes the waveform drastically while barely changing timbre.

Phase is not irrelevant, though: it determines transient shape, so scrambling smears attacks. And relative phase **between the ears** is exactly what [[itd]] is, so phase between channels is spatially critical even when phase within a channel is not.

sample-rate.title: Sample rate
sample-rate.short: How many samples per second represent the signal. 44.1 kHz throughout here.
sample-rate.body:
Sets the highest representable frequency at half the rate. It also sets the time grid: one sample at 44.1 kHz is about 23 microseconds, coarse compared to [[itd]] sensitivity, which is why [[fractional-delay]] is needed.

The same idea applies to derived series: the [[iacc-over-time]] series has its own effective rate set by the analysis window, which limits the [[rotation-signature|rotation frequencies]] it can resolve.

frequency-resolution.title: Frequency resolution
frequency-resolution.short: The finest frequency spacing an analysis can distinguish. Set by how long you observed.
frequency-resolution.body:
Roughly the reciprocal of the observation length: 20 seconds gives about 0.05 Hz resolution, 5 seconds gives 0.2 Hz.

This is why the [[rotation-signature]] measurement needs long passages. Looking for a line at 0.5 Hz in a 5-second passage smears it across a band far wider than the effect being isolated.

cents.title: Cents
cents.short: A logarithmic pitch unit. 100 cents is a semitone, 1200 an octave.
cents.body: Logarithmic, so the same musical interval is the same number of cents at any pitch. A few cents is a subtle detune; 10 to 20 cents is clearly audible as chorusing when copies are summed.

rms.title: RMS
rms.short: Root mean square: the average magnitude of a signal, a rough proxy for level.
rms.body:
Square every sample, average, take the square root. Unlike a plain average it does not cancel; unlike [[peak]] it reflects sustained level.

Frequency-blind, which is why [[lufs]] is preferred here: two signals at identical RMS can differ audibly in loudness if their spectra differ, and decorrelation methods do change spectral balance.

peak.title: Peak level
peak.body:
Matters for clipping, not for loudness. A signal can have a high peak and sound quiet, or the reverse, depending on density.

Renders here are normalized so the peak sits below full scale. Normalization is applied **once across a whole set** of variants rather than per variant, so that it does not itself introduce level differences between things being compared.

lufs.title: LUFS
lufs.grounding: ITU-R BS.1770, the broadcast loudness standard, defines the measure and its K-weighting.
lufs.short: Loudness Units relative to Full Scale: a perceptually weighted loudness measure.
lufs.body:
Applies [[k-weighting]] before measuring power, so it tracks perceived loudness rather than raw energy.

Used here as the default for [[level-matching]], because decorrelation methods differ in spectral balance and a frequency-blind measure would leave audible loudness differences between conditions.

k-weighting.title: K-weighting
k-weighting.short: The frequency weighting inside a LUFS measurement.
k-weighting.body:
Two filters in series: a high shelf approximating the head's acoustic effect, and a high-pass discounting very low frequencies that contribute little to perceived loudness.

The result agrees with listeners better than unweighted power, especially when comparing sounds of different spectral shape.

level-matching.title: Level matching
level-matching.grounding: Standard requirement in audio listening-test methodology; see ITU-R BS.1116 for the general protocol.
level-matching.short: Making conditions equally loud, so loudness does not decide the comparison.
level-matching.body:
**The most important methodological control in the instrument.** Louder reliably sounds better, wider and more impressive, so any uncontrolled level difference will dominate the judgement and produce a confident wrong conclusion.

Three properties are enforced. Matching is done in [[lufs]] rather than [[rms]], accounting for spectral differences. It is done **locally**, against the same passage played untreated, so the music keeps its dynamics instead of every region being flattened to a whole-track average. And every decorrelation control preserves per-source level by construction, so no control doubles as a volume control.

normalization.title: Normalization
normalization.short: Scaling a render so its peak sits at a fixed point below full scale.
normalization.body:
The subtlety is **when** it is applied. Normalizing each variant separately would undo [[level-matching]], because a variant with a higher crest factor would be scaled down more and end up quieter.

So a set of variants is normalized by a single shared factor derived from the loudest, preserving the relationships that matching established.

equal-power-crossfade.title: Equal-power crossfade
equal-power-crossfade.short: A fade that holds total power constant rather than total amplitude.
equal-power-crossfade.body:
When crossfading between **uncorrelated** signals, a linear fade dips about 3 dB in the middle, because uncorrelated signals add in power rather than amplitude. An equal-power fade, following a sine and cosine pair, keeps the sum steady.

It matters here because decorrelated material is close to uncorrelated, so the linear-fade dip would be at its worst, and an audible dip at every switch would be mistaken for a property of the treatment. For highly correlated signals the opposite holds and equal-power bumps up instead, which is why the fade is kept short.

iacc.title: Interaural cross-correlation coefficient (IACC)
iacc.grounding: Standard in room acoustics. Hidaka, Beranek and Okano (1995, JASA) on interaural cross-correlation and its relation to spatial impression; Ando's work on subjective preference in concert halls; Beranek, Concert Halls and Opera Houses.
iacc.short: How similar the two ear signals are, allowing a small time lag. Near 1 is coherent and centred, near 0 is diffuse and enveloping.
iacc.body:
The [[correlation-coefficient]] between left and right, maximised over lags of about ±1 ms, covering the range of physically plausible [[itd|ITDs]].

It is the standard objective correlate of spatial impression, where low values are associated with [[envelopment]] and [[apparent-source-width|width]].

**Read it with care.** It is not a rotation detector, it has a substantial [[noise-floor]], and it disagrees with the ear in specific ways. See [[metric-vs-percept]].

iacc-over-time.title: IACC over time
iacc-over-time.short: IACC measured in successive short windows instead of once over everything.
iacc-over-time.body:
A single number over a whole passage averages away everything that changes, which here is the interesting part.

The window length is a tradeoff: shorter windows track faster changes but give noisier estimates and worse [[frequency-resolution]] in any subsequent analysis. The series has its own effective [[sample-rate]], one over the window length, which caps the rotation rates that can be examined.

octave-bands.title: Octave bands
octave-bands.short: Splitting a measurement into bands each spanning a doubling of frequency.
octave-bands.body:
Roughly matches how hearing organises frequency, and is the convention in room acoustics.

Broadband [[iacc]] hides where the coherence went. Per-band IACC shows it, and the low bands are where decorrelation costs most: no [[head-shadow]] means no [[ild]] to carry a position. See [[bass-coherence]].

confound.title: Confound
confound.short: A second thing that changed at the same time, which could explain the result instead.
confound.body:
If two conditions differ in treatment **and** in loudness, and one sounds better, you cannot say which difference did it.

This instrument controls several by construction: [[level-matching]] removes loudness, [[mono-dry]] removes the record's own stereo image, sample-aligned variants remove position-in-the-music, and the [[matched-control]] removes the music's own periodicity from the [[rotation-signature]].

The one it cannot remove is you: see [[experimenter-bias]].

matched-control.title: Matched control
matched-control.short: A condition identical in every respect except the one variable under test.
matched-control.body:
The general principle is standard experimental design. Its form here: for any motion claim, the control is the identical configuration, on the same [[seed]], with the motion removed and nothing else touched. Whatever the material itself contributes appears in both and subtracts out.

Motion is removed by freezing the component, which stops its clock and leaves every rate in place. Zeroing the rates instead would also remove the edge fade a wrapping lattice carries, and the control would then sit louder at its edges than the thing it controls for. Both routes are recognised as the same control, and freezing is the one the interface offers.

The instrument pairs these automatically and reports the difference. A difference near zero means no measurable signature, which given [[metric-vs-percept]] is a weaker statement than inaudible.

seed.title: Random seed
seed.short: The number fixing which random filters get generated. Not cosmetic.
seed.body:
Pseudo-random generators produce a reproducible sequence determined by their seed. Same seed, same filters, same render.

Because of the [[noise-floor]], two conditions compared under **different** seeds can differ by more than either control actually does. Hold the seed fixed when comparing two settings, or average across several when characterising one.

envelopment.title: Envelopment
envelopment.grounding: Listener envelopment (LEV) is established in room acoustics; see Bradley and Soulodre (1995, JASA) on late lateral energy and envelopment, and Beranek's work on hall assessment.
envelopment.short: The sense of being surrounded by sound rather than facing it.
envelopment.body:
Associated with low [[iacc]] and with late-arriving lateral energy.

For this project it is necessary but not sufficient. A fully decorrelated field is enveloping and that alone is easy to achieve; the hard part is envelopment that also rotates. Keep the two separate in listening notes, because it is easy to hear the first and report it as the second.

apparent-source-width.title: Apparent source width
apparent-source-width.grounding: ASW is a standard concert-hall attribute, associated with early lateral energy; see Barron and Marshall (1981) and Beranek.
apparent-source-width.short: How broad a single source seems, as opposed to how surrounded you feel.
apparent-source-width.body:
A source can be clearly in front and still seem metres wide. Width and [[envelopment]] are distinct qualities, both associated with reduced [[iacc]], and both distinct from [[localization]] accuracy.

The distinction matters here: a very wide source is still **localizable**, in that its middle can be pointed at. 'Cannot point at anything' is a stronger claim than 'it is wide'.

spaciousness.title: Spaciousness
spaciousness.short: An umbrella term covering both source width and envelopment.
spaciousness.body:
Used loosely in the literature, which is why the two components are usually named separately: [[apparent-source-width]] and [[envelopment]].

Worth keeping precise here, because 'it sounds more spacious' could mean either, and the two have different implications for whether anything is localizable.

coloration.title: Coloration
coloration.short: Unwanted change in timbre introduced by a process.
coloration.body:
The main risk when decorrelating. [[comb-filtering]] is the usual culprit, producing a hollow or metallic quality; [[micro-delay]] and [[micro-pitch]] are especially prone to it.

[[velvet-noise]] is preferred largely because it is close to colourless. If a treatment sounds worse rather than wider, suspect coloration before concluding the spatial idea failed.

source-distance.title: Distance
source-distance.short: How far a source sits from the head, carried by level and by near-field interaural level growth. It may reach zero.
source-distance.body:
Distance is set in metres, with 2 m rendering at unity gain. Each ear's gain follows the inverse of its own path length to the source, so a near source is louder and its [[ild]] grows beyond the far-field value, which is the near-field effect described under [[distance-hearing]].

**Distance may be zero.** At the head centre both ears are equidistant, so the interaural differences vanish and the source is heard as a centred, in-head image, which is what a mono signal is. Sources may therefore pass through the listener without artefact: the cues fade out as they approach rather than swinging wildly, which is what would happen if they were held at arm's length instead.

A ceiling limits the loudness of a very near source. It scales the two ears together rather than clipping each, so the level difference between them survives.

Absent: propagation delay, Doppler, air absorption, and reverberation. Distance here is level and near-field ILD only.

motion-coherence.title: Motion coherence share
motion-coherence.short: The share of a component's sources taking part in its motion, the rest wandering with no net direction.
motion-coherence.body:
A share of a component's sources is excluded from its motion entirely, whatever that motion is: they neither turn, nor flow, nor drift. They wander instead, on a bounded path generated from the [[seed]], so the setting renders identically every time.

This carries the [[random-dot-kinematogram]] manipulation over directly, and it is where the visual parallel holds tightest. There the proportion of coherently moving dots sets the strength of the global motion signal, and the threshold on that proportion is a standard measure. Sweeping the share here puts the same question to an auditory ensemble.

It applies to any lattice, so a drifting [[grid-lattice]] can be made partly incoherent exactly as a turning [[polar-lattice]] can.

It is independent of [[decorrelation]], and the two do different work. This share decides which sources share a direction; decorrelation decides whether a source has a recoverable position at all. A field can be fully coherent in its motion and still unlocalizable, or fully localizable and only partly coherent.

field.title: Field
field.short: The whole ensemble of sources considered as one thing.
field.body:
Every [[source|source]] a [[variant]] renders, taken together, across however many [[component|components]] built it. The premise under test is that the field carries properties, motion among them, that no individual source carries.

Contrast with the usual way of describing spatial audio, where each source has a position and the scene is the sum of those positions. Here the arrangement is built so that the individual positions are unavailable to the listener and only the ensemble remains.

source.title: Source
source.short: One virtual sound position in the field.
source.body:
Each source takes the same input audio, applies its own [[decorrelation]] filter, and is placed at an [[azimuth]] and a distance through an [[hrtf]]. Sources are virtual: nothing is actually there, and the ear signals are synthesized as though something were.

Count matters as much as placement, since an odd number around a ring avoids the exact opposition behind [[antipodal-cancellation]].

ring.title: Ring
ring.short: A single circle of sources: the simplest polar lattice, and the configuration this project began with.
ring.body:
One ring of a [[polar-lattice]], at a single radius. Sources sit at [[azimuth|azimuths]] around the head, evenly spaced, unevenly spaced, or listed explicitly.

Geometry is not cosmetic: an evenly spaced ring of identical sources cancels to a centred mono image, and odd counts avoid the exact opposition that causes it; see [[antipodal-cancellation]].

Rotation was the first motion studied here, and a turning ring remains the clearest case. It is one configuration among many rather than the subject of the project.

passage.title: Passage
passage.short: A time region of the track that gets its own treatment.
passage.body:
Defined by a start and end in seconds. A passage holds one or more [[variant|variants]]: the untreated original, and any number of treatments to compare against it.

Passages are the unit of comparison. Everything inside one is identical material, so any difference heard between its variants comes from the treatment.

variant.title: Variant
variant.short: One treatment of one passage: either the untreated original, or a configured field.
variant.body:
Variants of a [[passage]] are rendered over exactly the same span, sample aligned, and [[level-matching|level matched]]. That is what makes switching between them a fair comparison.

Switch between them during playback, because [[auditory-memory]] for spatial quality is short and a comparison made across a gap is far weaker.

mono-dry.title: Mono reference
mono-dry.short: Untreated regions play the same mono sum the spatializer receives, not the original stereo.
mono-dry.body:
The renderer builds its field from the mono sum of the track. If the untreated reference were the original stereo mix, switching between treated and untreated would change both the spatial treatment **and** whether the record's own stereo image is present.

With this on, only the treatment differs. The mono version is [[level-matching|loudness matched]] to the original so toggling it does not change level.

Turn it off only when you specifically want to hear the treatment against the real record.

symmetry-breaking.title: Symmetry breaking
symmetry-breaking.short: Anything that stops a symmetric lattice from cancelling to mono, which any motion needs before it can be heard.
symmetry-breaking.body:
Four ways, all available:

1. **[[decorrelation]]** above 0, the main control. Sources stop being identical copies, so they stop cancelling. This is also what makes them individually unlocalizable, so it does both jobs at once.
2. **Uneven [[azimuth|azimuths]]**, removing the exact [[antipodal-cancellation|antipodal pairs]].
3. **Per-source gain**, unbalancing the field even with identical signals.
4. **Per-component decorrelation**, letting one group stay coherent inside a diffuse one.

The requirement is not specific to rotation. A perfectly symmetric coherent lattice cancels whatever velocity it is given, so a drifting grid and an inward flow need the symmetry broken exactly as a turning ring does; see [[degenerate-ring]].

antipodal-cancellation.title: Antipodal cancellation
antipodal-cancellation.short: In an even ring, every source has one directly opposite it, and that pair cancels.
antipodal-cancellation.body:
A source at [[azimuth]] θ and one at θ+180° produce equal and opposite [[itd|ITDs]] and mirror-image [[ild|ILDs]]. If the two carry the same signal, their interaural contributions cancel in the sum.

This is why source counts here are odd. An odd ring has no exact antipodal pairs.

interaural-statistics.title: Aggregate interaural statistics
interaural-statistics.short: The pooled pattern of interaural differences produced by a whole field, as opposed to any one source's cues.
interaural-statistics.body:
For a single source, [[itd]] and [[ild]] point at a position. For a [[field]] of many decorrelated sources no single pair dominates; what exists instead is a distribution, summarised by measures such as [[iacc]] and its variation across bands and over time.

**The conjecture** is that motion can be carried by slow modulation of that distribution without any individual source's position being recovered. That is a hypothesis about hearing rather than an established mechanism, and it is the level at which any auditory counterpart of [[global-motion]] would have to operate.

component.title: Component
component.short: A lattice of sources with a motion field applied to it. A variant is a list of components.
component.body:
A component has two parts: a **lattice** that places its sources, and a **motion field** that moves them. Two lattices are available.

A [[polar-lattice|polar lattice]] is concentric rings: so many rings deep, so many sources around each. A [[grid-lattice|grid]] is a rectangle of sources spanning an extent in metres.

Motion combines freely on either. [[rotation-rate|Rotation]] turns the lattice about the head, [[radial-flow]] moves sources inward or outward, and [[translation|drift]] carries the whole lattice in a direction. Setting more than one at a time is the point: a [[whirlpool]] is a polar lattice turning and flowing inward together.

Sources **wrap** within the lattice, so one leaving the far edge reappears at the near edge and the count never changes.

Each component carries its own [[decorrelation]] or inherits the variant's, so a near group and a far group can differ in coherence as well as in motion. Components can be copied and pasted between variants.

translation.title: Translation
translation.short: Straight-line drift of a whole lattice. Carried strongly left to right, and barely at all front to back.
translation.body:
Drift is given as a velocity on two axes: positive x to the right, positive y ahead. A [[grid-lattice]] with a backward drift is the field-passing-the-listener case.

**Left and right travel** moves both [[itd]] and [[ild]] substantially and is presented well.

**Front and back travel** is another matter. The head model is front-back symmetric, so mirror-image directions produce identical signals, and a source crossing the median plane keeps both ears equidistant throughout, so nothing interaural changes at all. Such motion is heard only as a change of level and near-field balance. It remains worth presenting, since it asks whether approach and recession read as motion on level alone, but it should not be described as a front-back percept. See [[front-back-measured]].

Measured [[sofa|HRTFs]] would change this.

polar-lattice.title: Polar lattice
polar-lattice.short: Concentric rings of sources: a number of rings across a radial band, with a number of sources around each.
polar-lattice.body:
Rings are spaced evenly across the band between the inner and outer radius, at half-steps rather than at the endpoints so that the outermost ring does not sit where the innermost one wraps to.

One [[ring]] at a single radius is the simplest case and was the original configuration this project studied. Several rings make a field with depth, and give [[radial-flow]] something to carry.

Ring stagger rotates each successive ring, which breaks the alignment that would otherwise put sources on shared radial spokes.

grid-lattice.title: Grid lattice
grid-lattice.short: A rectangle of sources spanning an extent in metres, which wraps as it drifts.
grid-lattice.body:
Sources sit on a rectangular grid centred on the listener, so many columns across and rows deep, spanning a stated extent. Giving the grid a drift velocity carries the whole lattice past the listener, and because it wraps, the field is endless: a source leaving the back edge reappears at the front.

The motivating image is driving through a space with sources placed at regular intervals. It is the configuration for asking whether [[translation]] can be perceived without localization, in the same way a turning [[polar-lattice]] asks it of rotation.

Rotation and [[radial-flow]] still apply to a grid, about the listener, so a drifting grid can also turn.

whirlpool.title: Whirlpool
whirlpool.short: A polar lattice turning and flowing inward at once, with inner rings turning faster than outer ones.
whirlpool.body:
Not a separate pattern but a combination: set a [[polar-lattice]] rotating, give it an inward [[radial-flow]], and set the outer rotation rate lower than the inner one. Rings then wind inward while the inner ones outrun the outer ones.

Each source keeps the angular rate of the radius it started at rather than picking up the local rate as it travels. That is a simplification: a real vortex conserves angular momentum, so a particle spun faster as it fell inward. The stateless version is reproducible and adequate for asking whether the pattern is perceived as one motion or as two.

It is the clearest case of the general point that motions compose within a single component.

radial-flow.title: Radial flow
radial-flow.short: Sources travelling inward or outward, wrapping at the limits of the band.
radial-flow.body:
On a [[polar-lattice]] this moves whole rings inward or outward together, so a ring reaching the inner limit reappears at the outer one and the flow is endless rather than emptying out. On a [[grid-lattice]] it changes each source's distance while leaving its direction unchanged, drawing the whole grid toward the listener or away from them.

Sources fade briefly at each limit, which keeps the wrap from being heard as a click while leaving every source present throughout.

Distance is carried by level and by the near-field growth of the [[ild]]; see [[source-distance]]. With no reverberation the cue is thin, so radial motion is a weaker percept than lateral motion.

Inward and outward are worth treating as separate conditions, since approach and recession are not symmetric in perception.

phenomenology.title: Phenomenology
phenomenology.grounding: Husserl's Logical Investigations and Ideas I for the method; Merleau-Ponty's Phenomenology of Perception for the embodied treatment of space; Gurwitsch's The Field of Consciousness for figure and ground.
phenomenology.short: The systematic study of the structure of experience, as distinct from the study of the stimulus or the mechanism.
phenomenology.body:
A discipline concerned with how things are given in experience: what is attended, what forms the background, and what a property is experienced as belonging to.

It bears directly on this project because the question here is whether a particular experience is available, not whether a signal difference is detectable. A listener could tell two renders apart on a timbral cue while hearing no motion at all, and that would pass a discrimination test while missing the point.

See [[micro-phenomenology]] for the interview technique and [[neurophenomenology]] for the pairing of first-person report with measurement.

micro-phenomenology.title: Micro-phenomenology
micro-phenomenology.grounding: Petitmengin (2006, Phenomenology and the Cognitive Sciences) on describing subjective experience; Petitmengin, Remillieux and Valenzuela-Moguillansky (2019) on the analysis procedure.
micro-phenomenology.short: A structured interview technique for obtaining fine-grained descriptions of an experience without leading the participant.
micro-phenomenology.body:
The interviewer guides attention back to a specific remembered moment and asks about its structure rather than about its interpretation, avoiding questions that supply the categories being sought.

Relevant here because the blind test's fixed-response items necessarily impose categories, and whether those categories fit the percept is exactly what is uncertain. Applied to a few listeners it would produce an account of what the percept is like, which a discrimination task cannot supply.

It does not replace [[blind-testing]]: an unblinded interview collects expectation as readily as experience.

neurophenomenology.title: Neurophenomenology
neurophenomenology.grounding: Varela (1996, Journal of Consciousness Studies), 'Neurophenomenology: a methodological remedy for the hard problem'; Lutz and Thompson (2003) for a worked application.
neurophenomenology.short: Pairing disciplined first-person reports with third-person measurement, with neither treated as the arbiter of the other.
neurophenomenology.body:
The proposal is that trained description and physiological or signal measurement constrain each other, rather than one being reduced to the other.

This instrument already has the shape of that pairing: it reports [[iacc]] and related measures beside a listener's response and states explicitly that where the two disagree is informative rather than an error. Adopting the programme properly would mean improving the first-person half, which is currently a set of fixed-response items, to match the care taken over the measurement half.

unison-motion.title: Motion in unison
unison-motion.short: A group of mutually decorrelated sources travelling together as one.
unison-motion.body:
A [[component]] whose sources are each [[decorrelation|decorrelated]] from the others while all taking part in the same motion. The motion can be a rotation about the head, an inward or outward flow, a straight drift past the listener, or any combination, since the lattice and the velocity are set separately.

Two properties come from two separate controls. **Motion** comes from the component's velocity. **Unlocalizability** comes from the decorrelation amount. At low decorrelation the result is trackable objects moving around the listener; at high decorrelation they merge into a diffuse field, and whether that field still audibly moves is [[the-question]].

The [[motion-coherence|motion coherence share]] is a third and independent setting. It decides how many of the sources share the motion, where decorrelation decides whether any of them can be placed at all.

At the coherent end the configuration fails outright: a fully coherent evenly spaced ring is [[degenerate-ring|degenerate]] and carries no motion at any velocity.

waveform.title: Waveform
waveform.grounding: Standard material. Rossing, Moore and Wheeler, The Science of Sound, covers it at an introductory level.
waveform.short: The shape of a sound plotted as pressure against time.
waveform.body:
Sound is a variation in air pressure. Drawing that variation against time gives the waveform, which is the most direct picture of a signal there is; everything else in this glossary is a way of summarising it.

Two timescales live in the same picture and are treated separately throughout. The rapid swings of the wave itself are its [[fine-structure|fine structure]]. The slower rise and fall of its overall size is its [[envelope]]. Hearing uses the two for different jobs.

A [[magnitude-spectrum|spectrum]] describes the same signal by which frequencies it contains rather than by its shape over time.

frequency.title: Frequency
frequency.grounding: Standard material. Rossing, Moore and Wheeler, The Science of Sound, covers it at an introductory level.
frequency.short: How many times a wave repeats each second, measured in hertz.
frequency.body:
One hertz is one cycle per second, and a kilohertz is a thousand of them. Human hearing spans roughly 20 Hz to 20 kHz, and pitch follows frequency: doubling it raises the pitch by an octave.

The period is the reciprocal, so a 1 kHz tone repeats every millisecond and a 5 kHz tone every 200 microseconds. Those numbers decide what the ear can follow in time.

Frequency matters here because nearly every mechanism in this instrument behaves differently at the two ends of the range. Timing cues work below about 1.5 kHz and level cues above, which is the [[duplex-theory]].

wavelength.title: Wavelength
wavelength.grounding: Standard material. Rossing, Moore and Wheeler, The Science of Sound, covers it at an introductory level.
wavelength.short: The distance one cycle of a wave spans as it travels.
wavelength.body:
Wavelength is the [[speed-of-sound|speed of sound]] divided by the [[frequency]]. At 343 m/s a 100 Hz tone spans about 3.4 metres and an 8 kHz tone about 4 centimetres.

Comparing that distance against the width of a head decides most of what follows. A wave far longer than the head bends around it and reaches both ears at nearly the same level; a wave shorter than the head is blocked and leaves a shadow behind it. That is where the [[ild]] comes from and why it depends on frequency; see [[diffraction]] and [[head-shadow]].

The same comparison sets where interaural timing turns ambiguous, since a delay longer than one cycle can no longer be told apart from a delay of one cycle plus a little more.

amplitude.title: Amplitude
amplitude.grounding: Standard material. Rossing, Moore and Wheeler, The Science of Sound, covers it at an introductory level.
amplitude.short: How large a wave's swing is, and so how loud it sounds.
amplitude.body:
The size of the pressure variation. Amplitude relates to loudness, though not in proportion, which is why levels are quoted in [[decibel|decibels]] rather than as raw numbers.

How amplitude changes across a sound is its [[envelope]]. Sudden changes are [[transient|transients]].

phase.title: Phase
phase.grounding: Standard material. Rossing, Moore and Wheeler, The Science of Sound, covers it at an introductory level.
