phase.short: Where a wave sits within its cycle at a given instant.
phase.body:
Two waves of the same [[frequency]] can be aligned or offset from one another, and phase names that offset, usually as an angle with a full cycle at 360 degrees.

It carries the interaural timing cue, since a delay between the ears appears as a phase difference at each frequency; see [[itd]]. It also decides what happens when signals are added together: aligned waves reinforce and opposed ones cancel, which is the mechanism behind [[comb-filtering]] and behind the collapse of a [[degenerate-ring|coherent symmetric ring]].

Hearing is largely insensitive to the absolute phase of a steady sound, and that insensitivity is what makes [[allpass-filter|allpass]] decorrelation possible: scrambling phase changes the [[waveform]] completely while leaving [[timbre]] nearly intact. See [[phase-spectrum]].

envelope.title: Envelope
envelope.grounding: Standard material. Moore, An Introduction to the Psychology of Hearing, is the usual reference.
envelope.short: The slow rise and fall of a sound's overall size, as distinct from the rapid wave inside it.
envelope.body:
Trace a line along the peaks of a [[waveform]] and the result is its envelope: the attack, sustain and decay of a note rather than the individual pressure swings that make it up.

The distinction from [[fine-structure|fine structure]] carries real weight in hearing. Interaural timing is read from fine structure at low frequencies, and above roughly 1.5 kHz that mechanism fails while envelope timing stays usable, because an envelope varies slowly enough to remain unambiguous; see [[itd]].

Distinct from the [[ir-envelope|IR envelope]], which is a control over the shape of a decorrelating filter rather than a property of the audio.

fine-structure.title: Fine structure
fine-structure.grounding: Standard material. Moore, An Introduction to the Psychology of Hearing, is the usual reference.
fine-structure.short: The rapid pressure swings of the wave itself, as distinct from its slower overall shape.
fine-structure.body:
The individual cycles of a [[waveform]], oscillating at the sound's [[frequency]], as opposed to the [[envelope]] riding on top of them.

At low frequencies the auditory system reads interaural timing from fine structure, following the wave cycle by cycle through [[phase-locking|phase locking]]. That is the most precise timing mechanism available to hearing, and it is why the [[itd]] is a low-frequency cue.

Above roughly 1.5 kHz it stops working, for two reasons at once. Neurons can no longer fire in step with cycles that short, and the [[wavelength]] drops below the width of the head, so more than one delay fits what the ears observe.

timbre.title: Timbre
timbre.grounding: Standard material. Rossing, Moore and Wheeler, The Science of Sound, covers it at an introductory level.
timbre.short: What distinguishes two sounds of the same pitch and loudness.
timbre.body:
Tone colour: what makes a flute and a violin playing the same note at the same volume sound like different instruments. It follows mostly from the [[magnitude-spectrum]], the balance of frequencies present, and from how that balance shifts over the course of a note.

It is the one quality every decorrelating filter here is required to leave alone. A filter that altered timbre would turn every comparison into a comparison of colour rather than of coherence, which is why the filters are approximately [[allpass-filter|allpass]]; see [[coloration]].

transient.title: Transient
transient.grounding: Standard material. Moore, An Introduction to the Psychology of Hearing, is the usual reference.
transient.short: A sharp, precisely timed event at the start of a sound.
transient.body:
A pluck, a hit, a consonant: a rapid rise in [[amplitude]] over a few milliseconds.

Transients matter more to this project than to most, because they are exactly what the auditory system uses to fix a position. A sharp onset reaches the two ears at two well-defined instants, giving an unambiguous [[itd]] and with it a pointable location. That is the localization the experiment is trying to remove, so material full of onsets works against the treatment however the parameters are set; see [[transient-material]].

Decorrelating filters also smear transients, since spreading a click across an impulse response is precisely what such a filter does; see [[ir-length]].

phase-locking.title: Phase locking
phase-locking.grounding: Rose, Brugge, Anderson and Hind (1967, Journal of Neurophysiology) measured phase-locking in the auditory nerve. Palmer and Russell (1986, Hearing Research) characterised its decline with frequency. Joris and Yin review its role in binaural processing.
phase-locking.short: Auditory neurons firing at a consistent point in each cycle of a sound, which is how timing reaches the brain.
phase-locking.body:
Hair cells in the inner ear release transmitter in step with the pressure wave, so the nerve fibres they drive tend to fire at the same [[phase]] of every cycle rather than at arbitrary moments. A fibre does not fire on every cycle, but the firings it does produce cluster at one point in the [[waveform]].

This is how timing survives into the nervous system. A fibre from the left ear and one from the right, both locked to the same sound, carry the interaural delay directly in the offset between their spike times, and structures in the brainstem compare the two to recover it; see [[itd]].

The mechanism weakens as frequency rises and is largely gone by 4 to 5 kHz, with the useful range for interaural timing ending nearer 1.5 kHz. A cycle at 5 kHz lasts 200 microseconds, which is too short for a cell to mark reliably. Above that range, timing comes from the [[envelope]] instead.

sampling.title: Sampling
sampling.grounding: Standard material. Smith, The Scientist and Engineer's Guide to Digital Signal Processing, is a readable introduction; Oppenheim and Schafer, Discrete-Time Signal Processing, is the reference text.
sampling.short: Representing a continuously varying signal as a list of values measured at regular instants.
sampling.body:
A microphone produces a voltage that varies continuously. Storing it digitally means measuring that voltage at regular intervals and keeping the numbers. Each measurement is a sample, and the interval between them is fixed by the [[sample-rate|sample rate]].

At the 44.1 kHz used here there are 44100 samples every second, so one sample covers about 23 microseconds. That figure sets the natural time grid for everything downstream, and it is coarse next to the roughly 10 microseconds of interaural delay a listener can resolve. Delays are therefore placed between samples rather than on them; see [[interpolation]] and [[fractional-delay]].

The rate also bounds frequency. A sampled signal can represent frequencies up to half the rate, which is 22.05 kHz here, comfortably above the top of hearing.

interpolation.title: Interpolation
interpolation.grounding: Standard material. Smith, The Scientist and Engineer's Guide to Digital Signal Processing, is a readable introduction; Oppenheim and Schafer, Discrete-Time Signal Processing, is the reference text.
interpolation.short: Estimating what a signal was doing between the instants where it was actually measured.
interpolation.body:
Samples give the signal at fixed instants, so any operation needing a value in between has to construct one. The crudest method draws a straight line between neighbouring samples; better ones use more of the surrounding samples and reconstruct the underlying wave more faithfully.

This is what allows a delay finer than the sample grid. Shifting a signal by two and a half samples means working out what it would have been half a sample later, which for audio is done by the [[windowed-sinc|windowed sinc]] method; see [[fractional-delay]].

The same idea returns when moving between measured directions in an [[sofa|HRTF]] dataset, where blending naively causes [[comb-filtering]]; see [[hrtf-interpolation]].

decibel.title: Decibel
decibel.grounding: Standard material. Rossing, Moore and Wheeler, The Science of Sound, covers it at an introductory level.
decibel.short: A logarithmic unit for level, in which equal ratios come out as equal steps.
decibel.body:
Sound levels span an enormous range, so they are quoted logarithmically. For amplitude, 20 dB is a factor of ten and 6 dB is roughly a factor of two, while 1 dB is around the smallest level change a listener notices on steady material.

Decibels always describe a ratio, either between two signals or against a stated reference. A single number here is either against digital full scale or in [[lufs]], which is loudness weighted.

The scale matters for comparisons. A treatment sitting 3 dB louder than another tends to be preferred whatever else it does, which is why [[level-matching]] happens before any listening.
